newsitem.title: USA: Boeing falls on high costs for new 747s.
newsitem.headline: Boeing falls on high costs for new 747s.

text.p: Boeing Co shares were down three points at 92-3/8 at midday Friday after the company said development of its next generation of 747 jumbo-jets could cost as much as $7 billion.
"Total non-recurring costs will be somewhere in the neighborhood of $5 billion to $7 billion," said Chris Villiers, a spokesman for Boeing.
In early September, Boeing told industry analysts at the Farnborough Air Show in England that costs for the new 747-500X and 747-600X aircraft would be "$5 billion or more."
"We originally said $5 billion plus. That was probably a conservative estimate," Villiers said. "We're now saying $5-$7 billion..."
He added that "we are working to keep it closer to the bottom of that range if possible."
Costs include research and development as well as tooling. When Boeing reports its results, R&D costs are counted against earnings, while tooling is amortized over the program length.
The 500X will seat about 460 passengers and fly 10,000 statute miles. The 600X will be able to travel 8,900 statute miles with 548 passengers.
The aircraft will be Boeing's flagship models for the new millenium and will compete with Airbus Industrie's A3XX family of planes, which will seat about 550 passengers.
Airbus has said the A3XX family will cost $8 billion to develop. Boeing has disputed the accuracy of that estimate.
The Boeing planes will feature a new wing and new engines, avionics systems and advanced hydrolics using new technology, as well as parts derived from both the 747 and 777 models.
The higher costs come as little surprise to some industry experts who took the original estimates with a grain of salt.

"Initially this started out as a derivitive of the 747 and now it's a new airplane that has some carry-over from the 747 and other planes," said Wolfgang Demisch of BT Securities. "This has been clearly visible for at least several months."

On September 6 industry analyst Jack Modzelewski of PaineWebber disputed Boeing's $5 billion estimate, saying in a research report, "It is our understanding that the actual estimate is closer to $7 billion."
Modzelewski cut his Boeing earnings estimate for fiscal 1997 to $4.75 a share from $5.20 due to the higher costs, but he maintained his attractive rating on the stock.
On Monday McDonnell Douglas Corp scrapped plans to develop a long-range commercial jetliner, dubbed the MD-XX, that would have allowed it to compete head to head with Seattle-based Boeing and Airbus.

Analysts said McDonnell Douglas balked at the investment needed to develop the range of aircraft it would need for such a competition. The analysts estimated the cost at up to $15 billion over 10-15 years.
McDonnell Douglas has bowed out of the race to build long-range, high-passenger-capacity aircraft, refocusing instead on its niche market of smaller planes.
